title: Rosalind and the Letters
premise: Astrid Lockridge, a cellist whose hands failed him during one catastrophic final performance twenty years ago, has built a careful life tending a small vineyard and teaching music to children who will never know what he once was. When a community pen-pal program anonymously pairs him with Rosalind Vane—the critic whose review ended his career—he begins an epistolary friendship without knowing her identity, while she, recognizing his voice immediately, conceals hers out of guilt and growing love. As the letters deepen into something neither can abandon, their offline lives collide at the vineyard's first harvest festival, where the truth detonates: she knew all along. Astrid must decide whether loyalty to the self he protected for two decades matters more than the truth that he is still capable of playing—and of being loved; he chooses truth, performing again at the harvest, imperfectly, with Rosalind in the front row.
about_author: Dominic Joubert is a former wine importer from Provence who turned to fiction after a decade of writing letters to strangers through a postal friendship society. He lives above a shuttered concert hall and claims the acoustics improve his prose.

chapters.title: The Last Train
chapters.summary: Astrid's POV. Twenty years after his hands betrayed him mid-concert, Astrid tends his vineyard in rigid routine, missing the last train home from a supply run—a small failure that rattles him more than it should. Emotional beat: the terror of imperfection governing a carefully small life.

chapters.title: An Assignment of Strangers
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. The town library launches a winter pen-pal program pairing anonymous residents; Rosalind, newly moved and lonely, signs up. The librarian's sorting error pairs her with Astrid. She recognizes his handwriting from old program notes. Emotional beat: guilt arriving before the first letter is even written.

chapters.title: Dear Stranger
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. First letters exchanged: Astrid writes stiffly about soil and frost; Rosalind replies with warmth and probing questions about music, which he deflects. Each hides more than anonymity requires. Emotional beat: cautious curiosity mistaken for safety.

chapters.title: What the Vine Remembers
chapters.summary: Astrid's POV. Pruning season; Astrid reflects on how he chose the vineyard because vines forgive bad years. He tells his pen pal, obliquely, about 'a friend who lost something on a stage.' Emotional beat: confession by proxy.

chapters.title: The Reviewer's Hand
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. Flashback to the night of Astrid's collapse and the review she wrote at twenty-six, hungry to make her name. We learn she has carried it through two careers and one failed marriage. Emotional beat: the corruption of power wielded carelessly.

chapters.title: Letters in Frost
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. Winter deepens; the letters grow intimate—Rosalind admits she once destroyed someone's career without knowing if they deserved it; Astrid admits he never played again. Neither connects the confessions. Emotional beat: two truths circling each other.

chapters.title: A Customer Named Vane
chapters.summary: Astrid's POV. Rosalind walks into his tasting room in person; he recognizes nothing, but she recognizes everything. She buys a bottle she won't drink and leaves quickly. Emotional beat: proximity as danger.

chapters.title: Small Safe Steps
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. Torn between withdrawing from the pen-pal program and staying near him, Rosalind volunteers to help with spring planting under a pretext. Astrid finds her competent, irritating, oddly easy company. Emotional beat: the enemy becoming a fixture.

chapters.title: The Cello in the Attic
chapters.summary: Astrid's POV. A storm damages the attic roof; Rosalind helps move things and discovers the cello under a sheet. Astrid's reaction is cold enough to end the afternoon. That night he writes his pen pal the longest letter yet. Emotional beat: the wound reopened by kindness.

chapters.title: Confession, Half-Written
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. Rosalind drafts a letter revealing her identity, burns it, drafts another. Meanwhile she begins quietly lobbying the village music society to host a summer recital, telling herself it's for the town. Emotional beat: amends curdling into manipulation.

chapters.title: Bud Break
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. Spring; the letters now arrive twice weekly and both admit, in writing, that the stranger has become the most important person in their lives. In person, Astrid and Rosalind share a first almost-kiss interrupted by a neighbor. Emotional beat: joy with a ticking clock.

chapters.title: The Librarian's Apology
chapters.summary: Astrid's POV. The librarian, tidying records, mentions the sorting error to Astrid—that his pen pal was assigned by mistake, not chance. He doesn't yet learn who. But he begins testing his correspondent with details only someone local would know. Emotional beat: suspicion as grief.

chapters.title: Tests
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. Astrid plants false details in his letters; Rosalind, sensing the trap but not its purpose, answers honestly and thereby confirms she knows things only an insider could. Both begin pulling back while wanting more. Emotional beat: trust eroding exactly as love peaks.

chapters.title: First Harvest Eve
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. The recital she engineered is announced for harvest festival—with a cello slot left conspicuously open. Rosalind realizes what she's done and races to stop it. Astrid, invited anonymously, sees the program and understands. Emotional beat: the trap sprung on its maker.

chapters.title: The Name at the Bottom
chapters.summary: Astrid's POV. Confronting the librarian's records, Astrid learns his pen pal signed her real name on the volunteer form: R. Vane. He reads every letter again with new eyes, seeing her guilt between the lines. Emotional beat: betrayal and recognition arriving together.

chapters.title: After the Last Train Leaves
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. Rosalind comes to the vineyard at night to confess in person; Astrid lets her speak, then tells her he's known for days. They fight—twenty years of ruin against one review, power against survival. She stays past the last train because he doesn't ask her to leave. Emotional beat: devastation that refuses to become goodbye.

chapters.title: Loyalty
chapters.summary: Astrid's POV. Astrid spends a bitter week deciding whether loyalty lies with his wounded younger self or with the woman who became his truest reader. He opens the attic, tunes the cello, and cannot yet play—but doesn't put it away. Emotional beat: choosing to stay in the room with pain.

chapters.title: What She Owes
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. Rosalind publicly resigns from the festival committee and offers Astrid the truth in print: a retraction of the review, offered whether or not he ever speaks to her again. Emotional beat: giving up control of the narrative as the only honest power left.

chapters.title: The Open Slot
chapters.summary: Astrid's POV. Festival day arrives. Astrid watches the empty cello chair from the back of the crowd, bottle in hand, and walks toward the stage as the announcer hesitates. Emotional beat: terror transfigured into decision.

chapters.title: Imperfect
chapters.summary: Astrid's POV, close second-person cadence. Astrid performs—his hands shake, he stops once, starts again, and finishes to a silence that breaks into something warmer than applause. Rosalind stands in the front row. Emotional beat: survival redefined as return, not avoidance.

chapters.title: The Letters, Bound
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. Weeks later, Rosalind gives Astrid the year of letters bound in linen, unedited, including the ones she never sent. They read them aloud to each other across the tasting room table. Emotional beat: intimacy rebuilt on full disclosure.

chapters.title: First Harvest
chapters.summary: Alternating POV, closing on shared narration. The vineyard brings in its first real harvest with neighbors' help; Astrid teaches a Saturday cello class again, badly and gladly. The last letter they write is addressed to each other, names signed. Emotional beat: the price paid, the truth kept, loyalty finally aligned.
